prose_changes.old: Parent of nearly everything on the map
prose_changes.new: The earliest layer on the map, which most later traditions claim as their root
prose_changes.reason: The census's own links do not support parenthood of 'nearly everything': the only documented line out of this movement is to the Roman church; no text links it to Alexandria or Edessa (see 2026-11-06 wanted texts). Restated as a claim later traditions make.

prose_changes.old: Almost every Christian tradition descends from these early gatherings.
prose_changes.new: Almost every Christian tradition claims a root in these early gatherings.
prose_changes.reason: Same reason: descent is stated as fact with no line to most traditions documented; what is true is that they claim it.

prose_changes.old: Overlaps post-apostolic-house-church in era and largely in people - Justin taught at Rome - but is a different thing: that entry is the church's internal life, this is the same Christians turned outward, addressing emperors and an educated public that despised them.
prose_changes.new: It overlaps the household churches of the same years, in time and in people. Justin taught at Rome, Theophilus was bishop of Antioch and Melito bishop of Sardis. But it is a different thing. The household churches show the church's inner life. Here the church turns outward, to emperors and an educated public that despised it.
prose_changes.reason: Removes a census ID and 'that entry' from public text. 'Largely in people' and 'the same Christians' rested on Justin alone; now names the documented overlap: Justin's own Sunday 'we' (1 Apol. 67, anf01 16502-16528), Theophilus 'sixth from the apostles' in the church of Antioch (Eusebius HE IV.20, npnf201 24429-24430), Melito 'bishop of the parish in Sardis' (HE IV.26, npnf201 25471-25472).

prose_changes.old: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move: rather than only denying the charges, most of them argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held, and that Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason rather than its enemies.
prose_changes.new: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move. Several of them, Justin above all, did more than deny the charges. They argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held. Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason, not its enemies.
prose_changes.reason: 'Most of them' overstates: Justin (2 Apol. 8, 13: 'seed of reason', 'spermatic word', anf01 17036, 17231-17236) and Athenagoras make the case, but Diognetus 8 scorns 'the empty and silly doctrines' of philosophers (anf01 2868) and Theophilus and Tatian are largely hostile. Also splits a 47-word sentence.

prose_changes.old: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down, and that Clement and Origen at Alexandria took much further.
prose_changes.new: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth', and he and Origen took the approach much further.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored Alexandrian text names Justin for this idea (2026-11-06 wanted-texts list), so the sentence no longer says they took Justin's argument further. It states the documented parallel: Clement, Strom. VI.7, 'if from any creature they received in any way whatever the seeds of the Truth' (anf02 46779-46780). The movement-level link stays the existing Tatian one.

prose_changes.old: who lost the post when the persecution began
prose_changes.new: who was still teaching there when the persecution broke out
prose_changes.reason: Lactantius says he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia when the church was destroyed (Div. inst. V.2.2; anf07 4487; Latin, Brandt line 22774). Neither he nor Jerome (DVI 80, npnf203 41034-41038: he 'betook himself to writing' for lack of pupils) says he lost the post; no repo-cited secondary found.

prose_changes.old: It bridges alexandria-catechetical, whose greatest teacher moved here, and jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity, which begins where this ends.
prose_changes.new: It bridges the Alexandrian school, whose greatest teacher moved here, and the Jerusalem church of liturgy and pilgrimage, which begins where this ends.
prose_changes.reason: The sentence printed two internal identifiers to readers; names replace them. Relationships unchanged (both carried by existing links).

prose_changes.old: The Hexapla, Origen's six-column Old Testament, sat here until the Arab conquest and was consulted by Jerome.
prose_changes.new: The Hexapla, Origen's six-column Old Testament, sat here. Jerome later searched these shelves and treasured copies of Origen made in Pamphilus's own hand.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text shows Jerome consulting the Hexapla itself, or the Hexapla surviving to the Arab conquest. Jerome's own words show him using the Caesarea library and owning Pamphilus's copies (De viris 75; Apology against Rufinus III.12).

prose_changes.old: Its natural relation to every other early entry is that they read it.
prose_changes.new: Its natural relation to the other early movements is that many of them read it. Origen, for one, knew the Protevangelium as the Book of James.
prose_changes.reason: 'Every other early entry' cannot be shown and 'entry' is internal language. Origen naming the Book of James (Comm. Matt. X.17) is the one reading now carried by a link.

prose_changes.old: And a third body is not Christian in origin at all: the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Life of Adam and Eve, the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works that survive because Christian scribes kept copying them, sometimes with Christian passages worked in, after Judaism itself had let them go.
prose_changes.new: And a third body is not Christian in origin at all: the Life of Adam and Eve and the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works that survive because Christian scribes kept copying them, sometimes with Christian passages worked in, after Judaism itself had let them go. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs may belong here too, but scholars still argue whether it began as a Jewish book or a Christian one.
prose_changes.reason: The Testaments' origin is disputed: the vendored ANF08 editor reads its author as a Christian (lines 632-655), and the project's own map data calls the question unresolved.

prose_changes.old: Pseudo-Matthew and its Carolingian abridgement that carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West
prose_changes.new: Pseudo-Matthew and its later Latin abridgement that carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source dates the Gospel of the Nativity of Mary to the Carolingian age; ANF08 (lines 35995-36002) says only that it is later, by another author, and passed into the Legenda Aurea.

prose_changes.old: Some of these works, like the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, were originally Jewish texts
prose_changes.new: Some of these works, like the Life of Adam and Eve, were originally Jewish texts
prose_changes.reason: Same reason as the Testaments change above: its Jewish origin is disputed, so it should not be the example.

prose_changes.old: Marian devotion in both East and West rests substantially on the Protevangelium of James: Anna and Joachim, the presentation in the Temple, the ox and the ass, all of it entered the calendar and the iconography from a book the church never accepted as scripture.
prose_changes.new: Marian devotion in both East and West rests substantially on the Protevangelium of James. Anna and Joachim and the presentation in the Temple entered the calendar and the iconography from it, a book the church never accepted as scripture. The ox and the ass at the manger come from Pseudo-Matthew, a later Latin retelling.
prose_changes.reason: Factual correction: the ox and the ass are not in the Protevangelium; they appear in Pseudo-Matthew ch. 14 (ANF08 lines 37907-37909).

prose_changes.old: The apocryphal Acts supplied medieval art and legend with most of what it knew about the apostles' deaths.
prose_changes.new: The apocryphal Acts tell how the apostles died: Peter crucified head down, Philip hung by his ankles. Medieval art and legend probably took most of what it knew of those deaths from them.
prose_changes.reason: The deaths are in the vendored Acts (ANF08 47557-47561, 48752); no vendored text documents the medieval reception, so it is stated as likely.

prose_changes.old: And the Jewish pseudepigrapha in this collection are the reason a large body of Second Temple literature exists at all - preserved, ironically, by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced it.
prose_changes.new: And the Jewish pseudepigrapha in this collection survive only because Christians copied them - preserved, ironically, by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced it.
prose_changes.reason: Narrowed to what the collection itself shows; 'a large body of Second Temple literature' is a wider claim no vendored text states.

prose_changes.old: Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously; Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled an anthology of his writings, and Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so.
prose_changes.new: Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus studied his books, and tradition credits them with an anthology of his writings. Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so.
prose_changes.reason: The project's own records hold the Basil-Nazianzen compilation of the Philocalia as Contested (records/cappadocian/source/cappadocian.source.origen-philocalia.md). Their study of Origen is documented (Socrates HE IV.26).

prose_changes.old: The tradition also fed directly into Egyptian monasticism, giving the desert its intellectual vocabulary.
prose_changes.new:
Whether the tradition also fed Egyptian monasticism is still argued. One modern reading finds Origen's ideas in Antony's letters. Athanasius tells instead of a boy raised at home by Christian parents.

The church of Alexandria itself remembered the school in two minds. Its History of the Patriarchs, compiled centuries later, condemns Origen's books but honours Dionysius as patriarch.
prose_changes.reason: The flat claim contradicted the existing Contested link to desert monasticism; rewritten to match it. Second paragraph names the existing Coptic 'argued against' link, which neither text named.

prose_changes.old: Basil's grandmother Macrina was formed by Gregory Thaumaturgus' disciples, and Basil appeals to his practice as precedent. Origen's reach runs through it in both directions - Gregory was his devoted pupil, Methodius his first serious critic.
prose_changes.new: Basil's grandmother Macrina taught him Gregory Thaumaturgus' words, and Basil appeals to Gregory's practice as precedent. Origen's reach runs through it in both directions - Gregory was his devoted pupil, Methodius one of his first serious critics.
prose_changes.reason: Basil says Macrina taught him Gregory's words (Ep. 204.6); no vendored text says she was formed by Gregory's disciples. 'First' critic is not shown by any vendored text.

prose_changes.old: He had fallen in with Origen at Caesarea instead, stayed five years, and left with a farewell address that is one of the warmest descriptions of a teacher anyone wrote in antiquity.
prose_changes.new: He had fallen in with Origen at Caesarea instead and stayed five years. The farewell address that bears his name is one of the warmest descriptions of a teacher anyone wrote in antiquity, though some scholars doubt he wrote it.
prose_changes.reason: The address's authorship is Contested in the project's own records (alx.source.gregory-address-to-origen: Nautin disputed it) and in the existing link note.

prose_changes.old: and became the first substantial critic of Origen, whose most devoted pupil had been Gregory.
prose_changes.new: and became one of the first substantial critics of Origen, whose most devoted pupil had been Gregory.
prose_changes.reason: Methodius's criticism is documented (Jerome DVI 83; Photius 234); that he was the first is not shown by any vendored text.

prose_changes.old: and became Origen's first serious critic before dying in the persecution around 311.
prose_changes.new: and became one of Origen's first serious critics before dying in the persecution around 311.
prose_changes.reason: Same as above.

prose_changes.old: And Methodius' Banquet is the foundation of the Christian literature of virginity - everything Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory of Nyssa later wrote on the subject is downstream of it, and its argument that chastity is a form of freedom rather than a deprivation began there.
prose_changes.new: And Methodius' Banquet is an early landmark of the Christian literature of virginity, a whole dialogue in its praise. Tertullian and Cyprian had already written about virgins. Jerome knew the Banquet by name, but how much he, Ambrose or Gregory of Nyssa drew from it is hard to show.
prose_changes.reason: 'Foundation' and 'began there' are contradicted by earlier vendored works (Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins, ANF04 2667; Cyprian, On the Dress of Virgins, ANF05 42953). No vendored text shows Ambrose or Gregory of Nyssa using the Banquet; Jerome names it (DVI 83).

prose_changes.old: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church; the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine passed into Arabic and back to Europe.
prose_changes.new: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church. Their translators later carried Greek philosophy and medicine into Arabic, and from there back to Europe.
prose_changes.reason: The translation movement into Arabic belongs to the 8th-9th-century heirs (the-church-of-the-east-under-persia's own legacy says so), not to this 200-410 community; the legacy field already says 'Centuries later'.

prose_changes.old: He wrote against Marcion, he was baptized in the Edessene church, and he ran a school whose hymns Ephraim would later complain were better than the orthodox ones - which is why Ephraim wrote hymns.
prose_changes.new: He wrote against Marcion, and he was baptized in the Edessene church. He and his school made hymns that Ephraim later accused of sweetening poison for the simple, and Ephraim answered them with hymns of his own.
prose_changes.reason: Ephraim's own words (Hymns against Heresies 53, quoted in npnf213 lines 11241-11244: 'He blended for the simple poison with sweetness') complain of sweetened poison, not of better hymns. 'Which is why Ephraim wrote hymns' overstates: Gwynn (npnf213 11225-11233) reports the biographer's claim that this controversy first led Ephraim to hymnody, but notes that the Nisibene hymns of c. 350 are earlier and not controversial. Sozomen III.16 and Theodoret IV.26 support the answer in kind.

prose_changes.new: raised in a sect of baptizers before breaking with it

prose_changes.new: In the East it lasted far longer. Many Uyghur Turks of Central Asia followed it, and it persisted in southern China for many centuries.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited text attests the Uyghur khagan's adoption of Manichaeism in the 760s. The vendored Yule-Cordier Cathay vol. 3 (1914), lines 3217-3223, citing von Le Coq, says many Uyghur 'were Manichaeans'. The China clause is kept unchanged.

prose_changes.old: Sits in the gap between post-apostolic-house-church, which ends at 200, and novatianism, which begins with the schism of 251 - the same decades those two entries bracket without covering.
prose_changes.new: The church of Rome after its house-church years, from about 200. The Novatian schism of 251 began inside it.
prose_changes.reason: Removes census ids and cataloguing language ('entries bracket'); keeps the two relations the existing links carry (continued from the house churches; Novatian schism began inside it).

prose_changes.old: became bishop of Rome and led a congregation through open arguments over whether the gravely lapsed could ever be restored, and how to speak of Father and Son without naming two Gods.
prose_changes.new: became bishop of Rome. He led his congregation through open arguments over grave sin after baptism, and over speaking of Father and Son without naming two Gods.
prose_changes.reason: Known open item (2026-11-06 README): Hippolytus's charge against Callistus concerned forgiving grave (sexual) sin after baptism (Ref. IX.7, anf05 lines 13871-13875), not the lapsed, whose crisis follows Decius (250). Split the 45-word sentence.

prose_changes.old: The questions argued here did not go away: whether the church can restore the gravely lapsed is what the Novatian schism of 251 and the Donatist controversy of the next century are both about, and Rome's answer - that it can - is the one the Western church kept.
prose_changes.new: The questions argued here did not go away. After the persecution of 250, Rome had to decide whether Christians who had sacrificed could be restored. The quarrel split the city in the Novatian schism of 251. Rome's answer - that they could - is the one the Western church kept.
prose_changes.reason: Same open item: the lapsed question belongs to 250-251 (Eusebius HE VI.43, npnf201 lines 38265-38294), not to Callistus. Drops the Donatist clause (see disposition). Split into short sentences.

prose_changes.old: Rigorist parallel communion; redundancy risk vs. Donatism noted if revisited
prose_changes.new: A strict church that broke from the Roman majority in 251. It lived on beside the majority for centuries.
prose_changes.reason: Removes internal cataloguing note ('redundancy risk vs. Donatism noted if revisited'); states the relation the existing roman-church-third-century--novatianism link carries.

prose_changes.old: A named neighbor within the milieu of the earliest scattered house churches.
prose_changes.new: In the late second century the faithful of Roman Asia met many times to judge it. They cast it out.
prose_changes.reason: Replaces cataloguing language ('named neighbor within the milieu') with the relation the new post-apostolic-house-church--montanism-the-new-prophecy link documents (HE V.16.10; anf07 line 11308).

prose_changes.old: Imperial suppression under Justinian in the sixth century finished it, its own writings were destroyed, and what remains is a handful of quoted oracles plus a body of Phrygian gravestone inscriptions whose Montanist identity is itself argued over.
prose_changes.new: Under Justinian in the sixth century the empire moved to crush it. Procopius says the Montanists of Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and set them alight. Its own writings were destroyed. What remains is a handful of quoted oracles plus a body of Phrygian gravestone inscriptions whose Montanist identity is itself argued over.
prose_changes.reason: 'Finished it' is more than the vendored source shows: Procopius (Secret History XI, lines 2168-2197) describes the campaign and the Phrygian Montanists burning their churches, not the movement's end. Split the 45-word sentence.

prose_changes.old: Later renewal movements down to modern Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity have repeatedly been accused of reviving it, and have occasionally claimed the comparison themselves, though no historical line connects them.
prose_changes.new: Critics of later revivals have reached for the comparison. In 1743 Charles Chauncy likened the cries and falling down of the Great Awakening to the Montanists of old. No historical line connects any later movement to it.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited text shows Pentecostals or charismatics being accused of reviving Montanism, or claiming the comparison. Chauncy 1743 (lines 6300-6304) shows a critic making the comparison against the Great Awakening. Keeps the denial of any historical line.

prose_changes.old: Confirmed distinct from the Imperial tradition; Donatism contests its interval
prose_changes.new: The churches led by Cyprian at Carthage and Augustine at Hippo. From the 310s a rival Donatist church stood in the same towns.
prose_changes.reason: Removes cataloguing language ('Confirmed distinct from the Imperial tradition'; 'contests its interval'); states the Donatist rivalry the existing donatism links carry.

prose_changes.old: The North African church itself did not survive: the Vandals took the province in the 430s, and the Arab conquest of the seventh century ended Latin Christianity there altogether.
prose_changes.new: The North African church itself did not survive. The Vandals took the province in the 430s. After the Arab conquest of the seventh century, Latin Christianity there slowly died out.
prose_changes.reason: 'Ended Latin Christianity there altogether' in the seventh century is not shown by any vendored text; softened to a slow end after the conquest (consistent with latin-africa-under-byzantium's own text). Vandal invasion and siege of Hippo: Possidius, Vita Augustini 28, lines 3982-3985 and 4079-4083.

prose_changes.old: Cyprian's letters became foundational for Western understandings of the bishop's office and the unity of the church.
prose_changes.new: Cyprian's letters became foundational for Western understandings of the bishop's office and the unity of the church. Later, the Donatists quoted them in their own defense.
prose_changes.reason: Two-way check: names the relation carried by latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity--donatism--2 (Augustine, De baptismo II.3: the Donatists cite Cyprian's letters, council and authority).

prose_changes.old: became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline.
prose_changes.new: became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline. In Geneva, Calvin wrote that he could fill a whole volume with Augustine's words on God's choice of the saved.
prose_changes.reason: Two-way check: names the relation carried by latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity--the-reformed-cities-zurich-and-geneva (Calvin, Inst. III.22, lines 25388-25391). 'Election' replaced by plain words.

prose_changes.old: Rivals the early traditions anathematized and were shaped by
prose_changes.new: Rivals the early churches cast out and wrote against. Answering them helped shape those churches.
prose_changes.reason: Second-century churches expelled Valentinus and wrote against his followers (Tertullian, Prescription 30; Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.4; Justin, Dialogue 35); no formal anathema of the period is in the vendored texts.

prose_changes.old: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136 and, according to Tertullian, was nearly elected bishop there.
prose_changes.new: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136. Tertullian says he hoped to become a bishop, and broke with the church when a confessor was chosen instead.
prose_changes.reason: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4 (anf03_tertullian.xml 43109-43114) says Valentinus 'had expected to become a bishop' and broke with the church when another won it on a confessor's claim. Nothing there says he was nearly elected, and the passage does not name the see.

prose_changes.old: The ground third-century Antioch stands on, eighty years before it starts, and the seedbed of the controversy the Homoian and Anomoean disputes later assess. Its relation to modalist-monarchianism is symmetry rather than descent: Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism are the two opposite ways of declining the account of the Son that the century was working out.
prose_changes.new: Third-century Antioch was the seedbed of the fourth-century quarrel over the Son. Lucian's pupils led the Arian party, and three of them later taught Aetius, the first Anomoean teacher. Its tie to modalist monarchianism is a mirror, not a line of descent. Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism were opposite ways of refusing the account of the Son that the century was working out.
prose_changes.reason: The first sentence was garbled ('stands on, eighty years before it starts') and used internal language ('assess', a raw movement id). The rewrite states what the sources show: Lucian's pupils among the Arian leaders (Theodoret HE I.5; Philostorgius II.14) and as Aetius's teachers (Philostorgius III.15). The modalist sentence keeps its meaning with the raw id replaced by a name.

prose_changes.old: Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East and, on the account of the council that removed him, a salaried official of the Palmyrene administration that then governed it.
prose_changes.new: Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius, a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city.
prose_changes.reason: The synodal letter (Eusebius HE VII.30.8, npnf201 42104-42105) says only that Paul preferred to be called ducenarius; the tie to the Palmyrene administration is the editor's inference (note at 42105), backed by Athanasius's report that Zenobia supported Paul.

prose_changes.old: The council's rejection of the word 'homoousios' as something Paul had misused is a large part of why that same word was still suspect at Nicaea, sixty years later.
prose_changes.new: In the 350s, bishops wary of Nicaea's word 'homoousios' pointed back to this council. They said it had turned the word down, and Athanasius had to explain why.
prose_changes.reason: The only vendored witness is Athanasius, On the Councils 43-45 (npnf204 58972-59060), written c. 359: bishops cite the deposers of Paul as having said the Son is not coessential, and Athanasius, who had not seen the letter, explains it. No vendored source shows the point raised at Nicaea in 325.

prose_changes.old: The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused, which is a large part of why its adoption at Nicaea in 325 was so contentious, and why Eastern bishops who were not Arians could still be uneasy about it.
prose_changes.new: The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused. A generation after Nicaea adopted it in 325, Eastern bishops who were not Arians still cited this council when they balked at it.
prose_changes.reason: Same evidence as the why-field change: Athanasius, On the Councils 43 (npnf204 58972-58980) shows the council cited in the 350s by non-Arian bishops; nothing vendored shows it shaping the debate at Nicaea itself. (Score is for the whole legacy field after changes 6 and 7.)

prose_changes.old: The Antiochene exegetical tradition that Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom carry is usually traced back to Lucian's work on the text as well - which makes this century the origin of two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.
prose_changes.new: The Antiochene way of reading Scripture, carried by Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom, may also go back to Lucian's work on the text. No ancient source draws that line. If it does, this century began two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.
prose_changes.reason: The existing link (Inferential-Thin) found no source tying Lucian to Diodore, Theodore or Chrysostom, and no repo-cited secondary work states the 'usually traced' consensus. The prose now matches the link. (Score is for the whole legacy field after changes 6 and 7.)

prose_changes.old: Sits between latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity, which is Latin but Carthaginian, and homoian-arian-christianity, which is Danubian but a century later and beyond the floor. Its text reaches hieronymian-ascetic-literary by a route no other work in the corpus takes: Jerome edited it.
prose_changes.new: It sits between two neighbors. Latin pastoral Christianity at Carthage shares its language but not its region. Homoian Christianity shares its region: its leaders held sees in these provinces fifty years later. Its commentary on the Apocalypse reaches us as Jerome edited it.
prose_changes.reason: Raw movement ids and internal phrases ('beyond the floor', 'in the corpus') removed. 'A century later' contradicted the entry's own 'within fifty years' (Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, Athanasius Apol. c. Ar. 48). 'No other work takes this route' was a claim about the vendored collection, not about history; it is dropped.

prose_changes.old: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - passed through Jerome's revision into Tyconius and Augustine and became the standard Western reading of the book.
prose_changes.new: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - survived Jerome's revision.
